Chapter Eight: On the healing of the pubic area, the herb miquinaria, bladder-herb or henbane, dysuria or urinary difficulty, seat ailments, gout, pain of the knee, beginning contraction of the knee, a remedy for cracks in the soles of the feet, injuries to the feet, against fatigue, against the weariness of those who administer public affairs and bear public office, and concerning trees and flowers.

Chapter Nine: On a remedy for dark blood, fevers, leprosy, hemorrhoids or condylomata, excessive heat, injury to the body, lichen or mentagra, recurring illness, scabies, received wounds, joint disease, psora, festering sores now becoming worm-ridden, burning of the body, dire concoctions, a cut vein, swelling from phlebotomy, and lightning strike.

Chapter Ten: On epilepsy or the falling sickness, a remedy for fear or faint-heartedness, mental derangement, those afflicted by a whirlwind or ill wind, warts, the stench of the wretched, goat-like body odor, lice-disease and head mange, crossing a river or water, and sciatica.

Chapter Eleven: On remedies for new childbirth, cleansing of monstrous births, the womb of a woman in childbed, lumps of the breasts, and a medicine to stimulate milk.

Chapter Twelve: On childhood scabies or burning, and when an infant no longer wishes to suckle the breast on account of some pain.

Chapter Thirteen: On certain signs of approaching death.

Elm

Tlalhauenetl.

Remedy for a received wound

An inflicted wound is healed if you instill into it the juice
from the bark of the Elm tree, the root of the Tlalhahucnetl fruit,
wax ointment, and egg yolk.

47

[Nahuatl plant names:] quanhxoxicathi, tetzitzcathi, patlahuacxithi, colosxix, xuhiltemayh.

Joint Disease.

To prepare a poultice against joint pain, take cuauhxixicatzin, tetzitzicatzin, colosxixquitl, patlahuacxitzicathi, and xuhillemayh — these are herbs — along with serpents, scorpions, and centipedes, which are ground together in water and strained. Furthermore, the part of the body that has become stiff should be rubbed with eagle bone or lion bone; then it should be anointed with the poultice described above, mixed with honey. But if the arthritic or joint patient is troubled by only moderate pain, there is no need to anoint any part at all.

Elolapolin. Tlati can. Ahuitati tepitom.

Against Scabies.

When this roughness of the skin takes hold of the body, take the bark of cherry, oak, and cypress trees; hanexcia wood, bramble; roots of the herbs tlayapaloni, tlalhaueueti, yolohua xihuitl; oak apple leaves and the herb tleltlanquaye — these are placed in water and boiled together with broth and ground squirrel egg. The affected part of the body, the one having pustular sores, is washed with the broth; afterward the prepared medicine is applied to it.

48

Cacamallalm    hecapahiti

Against dyspepsia, that is,
difficult and troubled digestion

When someone passes stool with difficulty due to crudeness of the stomach, grind for him cypress nuts, laurel leaves, the stem of the herb Zacamallalm, the bark of itibi, the bark of the corafi tree, and the root of the herb tonatliub, which when touched reddens bright gold. Once ground, let these be boiled in acidic water with honey. The juice, when drunk, wonderfully aids in purging the bowel.

Tzihuac copoalli. Tlaco Ecapahtli.

When a vein that has been blocked now swells.

If it happens that a vein swells after bloodletting, the following should be ground together in water cooked with the shrub Tzihuaccopoalli, and Tlacobecapahtli, and the herb tehermil, the root of the herb Homen polipoloa, the leaves of the herb quauh yy autitli, and ahnyac tlatlangua, and the herb coyoxihmitl — these are to be ground together with egg yolk; afterward, water fragrant with incense is poured over them, and with this juice the opened vein is to be bathed.

Quezalmizquitl. Tlalzacapol. Cimati.

Remedy for Festering Wounds Already Infected with Worms.

When you observe that a wound is already crawling with worms, grind together the leaves of quezalmizquitl, cimati, tlalcacapol, and ueprum, also the root of tlaquilm and the bark of xilexochitl, and do this in our finest wine. The resulting juice is to be applied to the worm-infested part morning and evening. It is also of no little benefit to apply a medicine made from thorns, oak bark, and quezalysin, tlalpahtli, quauhpahtli, tlattanquayo leaves, and the root of tlalthauhenetl, ground up in water with egg yolk. This is to be used twice daily, morning and evening, until the festering dries up.

Tlatoe Xochitli [Nahuatl plant name].

For burns of the body.

A burned part of our body is aided by a juice made from Xohpalli, Teamoxtli, Amextli, Teximilli, Hecapahtli, Texiyoll, and Hunigapihtli, with which the affected area should be anointed and rubbed, mixed with honey and egg yolk.

[heading:]
Against a lightning strike.

[body text:]
One who has been struck or hit by lightning shall drink a potion well prepared
from the branches of trees, namely Ayauh quahuitl, Tepapaqnil-
ti quahuitl, exceedingly green cypress, the fruits of yztauh-
yatl, the herb quauh y youhili and Teamextli. And this same
drink is to be given warmed by fire.

The body moreover shall be anointed with a poultice made from the herbs papa-
lo

loquitli, italhecayahlli, quauh yyonhlli, itallanquaye,
hiniginilgilbochill, yztac ocoxochitl: and likewise with all the herbs
over which the prepared thunderbolt has fallen. A few days after, he shall
drink water into which white frankincense has been cast.
The water, however, shall be boiled with white broth and a pale broth,
to which you shall add the bone of a Sinhecasle reduced to ash. You shall also mix in
a little of the above-mentioned indigo. Furthermore, you shall instill into the nostrils a medicine
composed of white pearl, the root of tlahllahcotic,
and all the small herbs that grow in the Garden where a fire
has at some time been lit. He shall also be fumigated
with white frankincense thrown upon coals, with the wax preparation called
aochiocokotl, and with the herb quauh yyaublli, which has a pleasant scent.

Chapter Ten, concerning epilepsy (the falling sickness), or the comitial disease; a remedy for fear, or faint-heartedness, for disturbance of the mind; for those afflicted by a whirlwind or evil wind; for the foul smell of the armpits of the sick; for the disease of lice; for lice of the head; for the calming of a river or water; and for excessive sweating.

[remainder of page illegible]

Quezalxahoyait. Ococol. tli. Tetzitzilm.

Epilepsy [Falling Sickness].

Against the sacred disease recently arisen, the following will be effective: small stones from the stomach of a hawk, the ears of the great horned owl and a rooster, the root of quezalxahoyait, stag's horn burnt to a whitish ash, white incense, the hair of a corpse, the flesh of a mole enclosed and burned in a clay pot — all of these must be well ground together in warm water. The epileptic person shall drink the liquid and vomit. And before this, it would not be useless for him to drink the juice of a shrub called tlahllacotic; its root must be ground.

Observe the moment when a seizure is about to come on. For at that very instant the epileptic must be made to stand upright, and his cartilage and sides must be pricked. Let him then drink a large amount of dog's bile, and at the same time let his head be bathed with a poultice prepared from zalachayait and the leaves of tetzitzilm and the herb or shrub acocohxihuill, ground in water. He shall eat the cooked brain of a fox and a weasel. And he must be fumigated with the pleasant smell of burned mouse droppings on hot coals, and with white incense, and with the feathers of the eagle called cozca quauhtli.

52

Quauhyayahunal.          Acxoyatl.

For one who has been afflicted by a whirlwind or an evil wind,
and how he shall be cured.

Let the one over whom a whirlwind has arisen drink the wholesome juice made in water from the root of the herb quauhyayanal and acxoyatl, first dug up and washed. The juice is boiled down, and he shall drink the decoction. For when taken, it drives out the evil air that has entered. Second, let him drink ground stones dissolved in water: red crystals, white pearls, white earth, and the leaves of the herb tlatlanquaye, which you shall boil together with bile. Anoint him with the seeds of cypress and cedar, and the leaves of the tree quauhyayauhth, and the leaves of the herb xiuhecapahtli, ground in water, with a carefully prepared liquid of bile.

Pozoca xihmitl.

Wart.

For the healing of warts. If you apply the ground leaves of the Verrucaria plant in water to the warts, so that they rot and, being putrefied, are thus removed. It will also help to frequently bathe the warts with water in which a human corpse has been washed.

53

Cacaloxochitl. Necouhxochitl

A Remedy for Fear and Faint-heartedness

One who is fearful shall take a drink prepared from the herb tonahius, which further expels misery. The herbs tlanextia xihuiti and tlahauiti, and white earth, are to be dissolved in river water or stream water; to these are added the flowers of cacaloxochitl, cacauaxochitl, and itacouhxochitl. Anoint him with a poultice, which you must make from sulfur, the blood of a tick, the color of the worm senecioyolotli, and dung, along with lamium, swallow dung ground in water, and sea foam.

One who has been terrified by lightning or thunderbolt shall be anointed with the dried leaves of the tree that was struck by lightning and with all the plants that grow near it. Furthermore, the water used to dissolve the ointment shall have a sour taste.

Cacauaxochitl chili. Yolloxochitl chili.

Against sudden death of the mind

He who is afflicted in his precious mind: let him grind the roots of tlah tlacolic in heated water and drink the juice and vomit. A few days later, let the flowers of yolloxochitl and cacauaxochitl, along with their barks and roots, be ground in water; let him drink the juice before eating, so that the evil humor occupying the chest may be driven down deeply. Third, grind together the small stones found in the birds xiuhquecholtotl and tlapalototl, tlahuitl, the precious stones tlahcalhuam, estell, and pearl in water. He shall drink half of this liquid, and the other half shall be poured repeatedly over his head. When this is done, he shall carry in his hands a small stone found in the tooth of the huaelli, which resembles bile at night; for by this carrying and drinking he will recover and be restored to soundness of mind. Furthermore, anoint the crown of the head with deer brain and cahimbe applied abundantly all over, along with morqua and human hair. Around the neck he shall carry a small stone found in the tooth of a swallow.

Totoloskim. Tonacaxochitl. Ayauhtonan.

Against the stench of the sick.

This offensive odor is removed by anointing the body with a preparation of the herbs ayauhtonanxochitl, papaloquilitl, and coinbecapahili, in the juice of their crushed leaves. One may also use the juice of the leaves and flowers of otoxochitl, tonacayxochitl, totolockim, and spikenard.

Chiyaua xihuitl.

Hircus or tragus of the armpit.

A notably smelly and goat-scented ingredient of the bath preparation, where it very carefully cleans the hair of the armpits. The herb Chiyaua xihuitl is indeed beneficial as a wash, as testified by its use on human bone and soot, which is freshly drawn from the body, and by the juice of all odorous plants and herbs, by which the goat-like odor may be eliminated.

Louse Disease

A multitude of lice will not afflict the body when one drinks a liquor made from the fresh horn of a deer, prepared in our local wine or in the finest oil. Moreover, you shall drink it as frequently as possible.

Zohzoyatic.

A lousy head.

A remedy prepared from the roots of the zohzoyatic plant, ground in bitter water, with the herb yzlauh yalt, goose fat or grease, the head of a mouse reduced to ash, and straws taken from a swallow's nest, which you shall also grind. This medicine you shall pour upon the head.

Tepepapaloquilitl

Tepepapaloquilitl.
A remedy for one who must cross a river or water.

Whoever wishes to cross a river or body of water shall moisten his chest with the liquid of crushed herbs steeped in water — yyauhitl and tepepapaloquilitl. In his hand he shall carry a beryl stone, an oyster with its head and entrails, a sardonyx, and the eyes of a large fish held closed in his mouth.

[The text is too faded and illegible to provide a reliable translation. Only the word "Fructus" (meaning "Fruit" or "Fruits") can be identified with confidence as a section heading within the body of the text.]

Mecaxochitl. Tlilxochitl. Huey ynacozti. Copalxocotl.

The support of hunters.

The dried flowers of mecaxochitl, tlilxochitl, the bark of the huey nacaztli tree and of copalxocotl and atoyaxocotl, the leaves of the axocotl tree, the white resinous substance, the seed of xochiocochitl, and yolloxochitl — let these be ground until they become a powder. The powder thus made is placed inside the hollow of the very well-known and most fragrant flower huacalxochitl, so that they may absorb and breathe out the sweetest scent of that flower. Then finally take the most praised flower yolloxochitl, hollow it out properly, place the health-giving powder into the cavity thus made, and hang it from a cord around the neck.

Chapter Eleven, concerning remedies for recent
childbirth, for menstruation, for washing of the belly,
for the woman in childbed, for tumors of the breasts, and a medicine
for attracting milk:—

[body text illegible]

Quauhalac. Cihuapahtli. Quetzalahicexotl.
Hinae.

A remedy for recent childbirth

If a woman is suffering difficulty in giving birth, so that she may hold and deliver her infant with little pain, she should drink a medicine made from the bark of the quauhalac tree boiled in water, together with the herb Cihuapahtli, a small stone called zotett, and the tail of the little creature called tlaquatzin [opossum]. She should carry the herb tlanextica in her hand. Furthermore, let the feathers and bones of an eagle's wing, the tree quetzalaexotl, deer hide, the bile of a rooster and hen, the bile of a hare, and dried onions be burned together; to these add salt, the fruit called in our tongue Nochili [nopal fruit], and otli. Let these aforesaid things be warmed and the body anointed with their juice. She should eat cooked flesh seasoned with sulphur, and smaragdine stones are firmly bound to the shoulders. She may also take in sweet local wine the ground fibers of a kite's dung and the tail juice of the tlaquatzin. Also, let the stalk of xaltomali, the tail of the tlaquatzin, and the leaves of cihuapahtli be ground, and with their liquid let the womb be moistened. Likewise grind the large tail of the tlaquatzin, and with the juice of the herb cihuapahtli, administered as an enema, wash or anoint the area.

Xinheloquiliti. Tlacopopoti.

Washing of the belly of a woman in labor.

The belly of a woman near childbirth is to be washed with the juice of the herbs xinheloquiliti, tlacopopoti, centzontxochitl, xinpali, lanj, which you shall grind in spring water together with the stone ezteli and teslahuitl. With this same liquid the feet are also to be washed repeatedly. If the birth of the child is now imminent, one also grinds yztac huiqualnitl, malinalli, white stone, white nitium, pine, palm, and ezteli in water in a sufficient quantity.

Iztachinzquahvitl Ayohnelhuatl

Into the womb, moreover, you shall insert the ground herb ayonelhuatl, eagle dung, potherbs, the root of quanhtlahnac, and the stone eztell, by which the pain will be relieved.

pocahnaliz xiuhtotli.    Xomalin.  Totec yxiuh.

Tumor of the breast.

A swelling growth of the breasts is treated with the leafy cedar and its cones, the leaves and roots of quauhyygauhtli, the herb elocacall, and likewise pocahnalizxiuhtontli and totec yxiuh. The juice suppresses it, if with it the affected breasts are anointed.

Tohinyoxihuitl    Memeyaxihuitl

Medicine to promote milk flow

When milk flows with difficulty, the herb chichiltic xiuhtonth, which in its sharpness resembles vinegar sauce, along with tohm yo xihuitl and crystal, are ground in octh [pulque] and boiled. This drink is to be taken frequently. Furthermore, the herb memeya xiuhtonth is rubbed in a pot; let even the nursing woman drink its dried form, and let her take a bath, and then drink another drink made from grain. When she goes out, let her take the viscous water of boiled grain to drink.

60

Tohinyoxihuitl     Memeyaxihuitl

Drawing milk / inducing milk

When milk flows with difficulty, the herb chichiltic xiuhtonth, which in its sharpness resembles vinegar, along with tohinyoxihuitl and crystal, shall be ground in water and boiled. This drink shall be taken frequently. Furthermore, the herb memexya xiuhtonth shall be ground in a pot, and even a woman shall drink its dried form; she shall take a bath, and then drink another potion made from grain. Upon leaving the bath, she shall take a thick, viscous water made from boiled grain.

The twelfth chapter concerning children with scabies, or burns, and the infant who no longer wishes to nurse the breast on account of some pain.

61

Acamallotell.        Coltokin.

Against burns in infants.

Siriasis, which is a burning affliction of infants, is cured if the body is anointed with a poultice made from the well-known seed michihuathlli, ground with red ochre and grain. The things to be combined are: the herb tlatlanquaye, the leaves of huitzihgilxochitl, the root of tlalahueuetl and tlayapaloni, the fronds of laurel and xinhecapahili, all of which must be washed with acidic water. The child should also drink a medicine made from whitish earth, small white pebbles gathered from the bottom of a river, the stone acamalletell and coltokim, the shrub tlalmizquitl, and ears of grain that are to be ground in water.
When an infant refuses to suckle from the breast on account of a certain pain.

If an infant is so afflicted that he now refuses milk and will not bring his lips to his mother's breasts, give him a drink prepared from the little herbs called teamoxetli and cotirmeis, with dried liver, and from a few of his own hairs clipped off, which you shall reduce to ash.

Anoint him with a poultice carefully prepared from the brain of a weasel and human bone ground together, which you shall strain through acidic water. ~ ~ ~

Chapter Thirteen, concerning certain signs of one about to die. ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~

Quetzalysin

A prudent physician draws his prognosis from the very eyes and nostrils of a sick person, not from his manner of dying. Thus, according to that well-founded opinion, red eyes indicate without doubt a sign of life. Pale and whitish eyes are signs of uncertain recovery. The signs of death are: a certain sooty color found in the middle of the eyes, the crown of the head growing cold or contracting into a kind of hollow, eyes turning dark and seeing little, the nose becoming thin and almost pointed like a twig, the jaws growing stiff, the tongue growing cold, the teeth dusty and exceedingly foul, no longer able to move or open. Likewise the grinding of the teeth, and that which flows from a cut vein

Blood that is pale or black is a messenger of death from the belly. Furthermore, the face growing pale, turning dark, and taking on one expression after another; and especially if words tumble out without sense, like a parrot, pouring them forth in no order.

In a woman, moreover, one special sign has been observed, namely if the buttocks, thighs, and sides are pricked as if by a very sharp thorn.

Yet against a desperate and hopeless condition, you may still instill into the eyes of the dying a medicine carefully made from precious stones — tlahcalhuahieztoll, pearl, and white pearl — ground to a pale powder in water.

Anoint the chest with a liquid made from pine ground in water, with laurel, and with the herb tonatiuh yxiuh, which you will gather in summer and store for that purpose. Prick likewise with a sharpened bone of a wolf, a bone of an eagle, or one of a white lion, or of that animal whose hide is mottled and speckled with a black pattern. To the buttocks attach the heart of an eagle, covered and wrapped in deer hide.

Finally, give as a drink a potion made from precious stones — white pearl, deep green pearl, emerald — pale earth of forest stones, and tlahcalhuahim, which you shall grind. Likewise from cypress cones, laurel leaves, the herbs tlanextia and xilimitl, tonatiuh yxiuh which glows like fire, the tree quetzalylm, and from the small stones which you shall seek in the gizzards of the eagle, quail, swallow, rooster, blackbird, wryneck, quecholtotoll, tlapaltotoll, nochitotoll, hummingbird, and dove — all of which you shall grind. And then—

...as is customary when fatal necessity is near at hand, and we are close to dying, blood flows most abundantly over the heart; and when it is distributed throughout all the limbs, we fulfill our mortality.

Joannes Badianus, Translator, to the candid reader, greetings.

Xiuhhecapalli . Yztac ocoxochitl . Temaxtli .

Treatment of the Head.

The shrubs xiuhhecapalli, yztac ocoxochitl, temaxtli, and the precious stones tellahuitl and yztactlalli, together with eztli and temamatlakin, mixed together in cold water, calm the heat of the head, and in warm water they cool it likewise. They are to be applied three times a day — in the morning, at midday, and in the evening — and the feet and neck are to be bound with a nerve or sinew of the throat and neck. The one suffering in the head shall eat onions in honey, shall not sit in the sun, shall not work, and shall not enter the baths.

Chipanac
xihuitl        Tlayapalsm    Tlalanenell

Domica

The leaves of the plant tlallanquaye, the root of tlalhauenell, tlayapalsm and
Chipahnac xihuitl, well crushed without water in the yolk of an egg, are to be applied to the head of a person carefully purged of pus, in the morning as well as in the evening; once this is done, the head is well covered. But if any part of the head should fester, it shall be washed with urine and the same remedy shall be applied.

Chipanac
xihuitl

Tlayapalsm Tlalanenell

For the Head

The leaves of the herb tlallanquaye, the root of tlalhauenell, tlayapalsm, and chipahnac xihuitl, well ground without water into an egg yolk, shall be applied to the head of a person who has been carefully purged of pus, in the morning as well as in the evening; once this is done, the head is to be well covered. But if any part of the head alone should be putrefying, it shall be washed with urine and the same medicine shall be applied.

quauhtlaxoxocoyolin

Dandruff or Alopecia

Wash the head afflicted with dandruff thoroughly with heated lye. Then a juice well pressed and strained from wild salad herbs, ground up, is to be poured over bald patches; once this has dried, the bile of a dog, fox, mole, hawk, swallow, merganser, quail, and of the white gicmilotl, mixed with wine dregs or ammi seed of Indian wine, is to be smeared on the head affected by alopecia. As a drink for the alopecia patient, let him take Indian wine warmed in unheated honey. Before the meal he should take great care not to fall asleep; and after the meal let him not go anywhere, nor walk about or run, nor exert himself.

Teconpahlli. Huitzquilit. Tequommayll.

[botanical illustrations]

Scabies (Scabrous head / Scalp Mange)

A scabious head, burning as if with coals and other such filth, shall be cleansed; then this poultice shall be pressed out: the root of tequommayll is taken, its juice shall be expressed, and then you shall anoint the scabious head on the temples and hands with this juice.

A scabious head shall be washed in a jar: then zachias, huitzquillit, teconpahlli, tequommayll, telzimxochitl, together with the barks of copalquahuitl and atoyaxocotl, ground up together, shall be applied to the head.

9

xiuh amolli

Hair loss.

The flow of hair is checked by washing the head, and if there is applied to it the herb named xiuh hamolli, ground and cooked in dog's or rabbit's urine, together with reeds and the small creatures called auae colott.

Cacau Angri
X ihiuitl tonalco mochiua hahualcho

For a broken head.

Dewy herbs that grow in summer, together with an emerald, a pearl, crystal, tlah calhnatzin, and ground earthworms, mixed with the soft yolk of a vein and beaten egg white, are to be smeared on the broken head; if the yolk cannot be obtained, the ash of a burned frog will serve as a substitute.

The second chapter on the treatment of eyes: on heat, on blood occupying the eyes, on glaucoma, on numbness of the eyebrows or rather the eyelids, on swelling of the eyes, on inducing sleep, on the imitation of drowsiness.

Remedies for the eyes.

For painful eyes, white frankincense and powdered dead earth, well ground together in dragon's blood and the white of an egg, applied continually as a remedy [illegible]
[illegible]

21

Xaltomatl.     Matlatxochitl.

[botanical illustrations]

Heat.

For an ailment in which the eyes become greatly inflamed, the root of this shrub is ground and instilled. The face moreover is to be wiped with the expressed juice of the shrubs ocoxochitl, snacalxochitl, matlatxochitl, and tlacotyzquatochitl. For irritated eyes, the leaves of the mizquitl tree and xoxouhqui matlatxochitl in a woman's milk, or

...with dew or clear ground water instilled will bring relief.
One suffering from eye disease should abstain greatly from lust, from the heat of the sun, smoke, and wind; and in food he should not take chilmolti as a condiment, nor eat hot food. He should wear a red crystal near the neck — he will not see white but black.
Sulfur is wonderfully beneficial for diseased eyes: for this reason it will be bound to the arm, and if the eyes are so diseased that they seem nearly used up, take a pearl, a pumice-colored crystal, a reddish oyster shell, the small stone found in the little bird called molototoll, the stone called tlahcalnakin, and the stone found in the crop of the Indian dove — grind these in the blood of a goose, woman's milk, and spring water, and having prepared it thus, instill it over the affected eyes.
But when something more deadly occurs, and from it the eyes begin to putrefy, there should be instilled into them a concentrated liquor made with a pod-shell, salt, and flour with spring water. If however this affliction has arisen from cold, it is remedied if a pumice-colored crystal is ground in the juice of the indigo plant and the liquid is instilled into the eyes.

Blood occupying the eyes.

This condition is cured if the eyes, suffused with blood, are sprinkled with powdered human ash and oil. By the same remedy also, argemata and white spots of the eyes, and diseased conditions of the eyes: the freshly ground shell of a walnut, together with its inner membrane, strained with ash in sharp or bitter water, left for eight days and thereafter instilled drop by drop, is very effective.

12

ohuaxocoyolin

Glaucoma

Pluck out a small fleshy growth arising in the eye by piercing it with a needle and drawing it forth; then sprinkle over the white of the eye a little ash made from human dung, together with salt. On the following day, apply to the same place the roots of our native salad herbs, dried in the sun and ground up.

51

Malinalli

[For] Calopthalmus and Ectropion

Rough teeth must be polished most carefully: once the tartar has been removed, they are to be rubbed with white ash applied on a small cloth dipped in white honey, so that an elegant cleanliness and natural brightness of the teeth may last.

Toothache

Against water under the skin
The fluid under the skin must be lanced and all the pus expelled. I am able to honor your beneficence. I can indeed give the greatest thanks to my patron, but I am far from being able to repay them. For this reason I offer, dedicate, and consecrate myself entirely, as much as I am, as your servant. And not to him alone, but also to you, my most illustrious lord, as the most earnest sign and testimony of singular affection. For I suspect that you have sought this little book of herbs and medicines so eagerly for no other reason than to commend the Indians — though undeserving — to the Sacred Imperial Catholic Royal Majesty. Would that the Indians had made a book worthy of the king's sight, for this one is altogether most unworthy to come before the presence of so great a majesty. But you will remember that we wretched, poor Indians are inferior to all mortal men, and therefore our smallness and slenderness, visited upon us by nature, is to be wondered at. Now therefore this little book, which by your name, most magnificent of all men, I am bound to dedicate, I beg you to receive from the hand of your little servant in the same spirit in which it is offered, or, what would not surprise me, to cast it aside as it deserves. Farewell. Tlatilulco. In the year of the Lord 1552.

These flowering herbs together with their shoots, which you shall gather in the morning before the dew rises, are to be pressed in spring water, clear and fresh. Each one separately in new jars or vessels, and left for one day and one night; to these shall be added the wood of huixquahuill, of red sap, that it may give them color. Likewise let the blood of wild creatures, namely tlaHauhqui ocelotl, cuetlachtli, mountain lion, ocolochtli, white ocelotl, and slaco ocelotl, be obtained. With these and the liquids described above let the body be anointed. Second, let precious stones — quetzalytli, eztell, tlahcalhuatyn, testalınill — and white earth and the small stones found in the stomachs of the birds huexoconauhili, huatli, and apophtli be cast into water —

...in which they should remain for one night, and a wholesome juice is extracted, with which the body is frequently washed. Third, the animal parts of the tlallauhqui ocelotl, yztac ocelotl, cuetlachtli, mitli, ocotothtli, coyotl — along with their brains and bile, and finally the ground brain, bile, and bladder of the yztac epati — are applied as a rub.

These remedies truly strengthen the endurance of gladiators' bodies, drive away fatigue for a longer time, banish fear, and fortify the human heart.

Furthermore, one who wishes to achieve the first — or indeed any of the five — restorations of this body should eat the flesh of the white fox or small white vixen, either roasted or boiled.

A remedy for black blood.

The leaves and roots of the plants huizquilit and tlallanquaye shall be cooked in water, to which shall be added a pearl, liver of lupin, and our wine. The patient shall take this juice little by little for drinking. He shall drink a juice pressed from diverse kinds of sweet-smelling flowers before meals. He shall walk in a shaded place, shall restrain himself from lust, shall drink wine as a nighttime medicine — indeed he shall drink nothing except as medicine. He shall devote himself to the most joyful pursuits, such as singing or vocal music, and to the playing of drums, which we are accustomed to use in public dancing.

Fever.

The appearance of a feverish person changes in many ways: sometimes the face turns red, sometimes dark, sometimes pale. The person also spits blood, vomits, tosses and turns the body this way and that, sees poorly. In the mouth, or rather on the palate, there clings now a bitter taste, now a sharper one, and sometimes a sweet one. A person in such a state clearly has a thoroughly corrupted stomach. If the urine turns white, the patient is immediately in danger, and medicine will be prepared too late. Therefore you will help him wonderfully if you grind together the herbs cehonxochitl, teoyztaquilitl, haquiztli, tlanextia ximitl, quauhtlahuiztlquitl, tonatiuh yxiuh, tlahcolto iecatl, mauatlanelouatl, vexoxochitl, çacamatlaln, the small shrub tlanextia qualuitl, also the small stones which are found in the stomachs of these birds: huitlalotl, huactli, tlatlalli, apopohtic, tlacahuitoll, Vexocanauhtli, xiuhquexboltotoll, tlapaltatoll, nochtotoll, acachanall, tolim, precious stones, green herb, pearl, emerald, sardonyx, and Xiuhitemolti, and calcined human bone. These [plants] are sought out by the heat of the sun fermenting. They are willow trees and laurel, and human bone, with whose liquid [the patient] is to be anointed. Colomecatl.

Hemorrhoids.

Against hemorrhoids, the stem of the herb Colomecatl is very effective. For when it is ground with honey in warm water, if the juice is drunk, it draws out the bile. Second, teohonatli, the herb that grows over pestilence, is prepared by decoction, so that that juice, which abounds in milk, may flow out. It is to be taken with cotton and dried a little in the sun, and drunk moderately, by which pale bile is drawn out. Within a few days the medicine heals what it would otherwise dissolve. Furthermore, a medicine is made from the herbs quauh yzeçochitl and a sun-dried bark, bitter when warmed. This indeed draws out the purulence and cleanses the belly of man. Before lunch, let him eat a weasel that has been killed and notably prepared, together with the heart of a dragon.

Chichic Texcalamatl.

Condyloma.

The bark of oak, the bark of huiiquahuill, and the barks of apollaxipetnalli and tlacoxiloxochitl are to be ground together. To these are added tlapalachi yotl and the substance we call in our language holli, the gall of an egg, the stalk of almond, the bark of yiquixochitl, and the leaves and bark of chichic texcalamatl. A preparation is made by drying in the sun, mixing things that need to be warmed, or preferably cooked. A cloth is soaked in honey, with which the condyloma is touched and rubbed. If this affliction is in the nostrils or near the anus, warm water should be poured over it, and it should also be washed with the juice from the bark of teo amotl, to which honey is added. Having made this juice into a softening medicine, the part afflicted with condyloma should be bathed with it as frequently as possible.

The herb italquetlal is ground in warm water and the juice is drunk.

Acacahōtl.

Excessive heat.

The body burning with fever is cooled by the roots of these plants, namely: xaliomati, tlacacamōhlli, ieconstaquilit, the stone smallotēll, estēll, tlalcalmagm, red earth, white earth, the small stones that form in the gizzard of the rooster, and noch totōtl — all of these are to be placed in water. The juice is to be drunk, and the patient is to be purged by enema. The potion, moreover, shall consist of the roots of haymal quilit, tlacacapacquilit, tolpatlactli, the fruits of tequmil, ystauboyotlh, and to this salt is added. The body is to be anointed with the sap expressed from acacapactliutlil, coyoxihuitl, tlathecapatli, tonahuhyxiuh, yztac oxbxochitl, cēganxochitl — these are herbs — together with bay laurel leaves, the fruits of tequmil, and the fruits of the fruit-bearing tree xexbxotl, the herb tohuaxoxocōtl, and pine needles. This medicine is to be divided. Some portion, not too much, is to be applied to the body as something quite thick. If the fever is excessive, let the liver of the heron, the bile of the huexxocanauhtli, the entrails of the quail, the bladder of the cochtli, and the skin of the pecōtli be burned. And these, along with the things mentioned above, are to be mixed together.

Remedies.

A body that has been beaten and badly treated shall be anointed with a poultice made from tlahcolteoquatl, contion xochitl, xiuhtotla, axocoll, tlayapaloni, xiuhtantli, moss of a certain tree, cypress nuts, nettle seed, and the tree ayauh quahuitl. One who has been beaten and afflicted shall drink a well-prepared juice made from the stalk of cohuanenepilli, tlanextra xiuiuitl, chicomacall, the flower of axocoll, and yzquixochitl, teltlahuill, aztell, teamoxlli, and the liver of the aquatic creature luexocamauhtli, and several tlah tlanche leaves, which indeed are to be steeped in sour water.

Aqualnitl.

Against scaly skin disease of the chin (mentagram).

For one suffering from this scaly affliction, grind together first: the bark of the wild cherry tree, the bark of the incense tree, quauh xoyotl, pemi, the flower of topozan and cacaloxochitl, oak, cypress roots and acorns, the leaves of the herbs tlatlanquaye, quauh yayahual, the herbs tepechian, coyoxihuil, aqualnitl, cedar acorns and leaves. With these, heated, the patient should wash himself, and the scaly part should be rubbed with that liquid. Then anoint with resin and rose resin, which is drawn from us by burning pine. With these things let the affected area be anointed, together with all the above-mentioned ingredients.

Cuecuechpahlli

A Recurring Illness.

One who falls ill again should, before a meal, drink the juice pressed from something very similar to teohamatl milk, which causes vomiting. On the third or fourth day, let him drink a preparation made from tonaliu, from the stem of xiuh herb, and itatlanquaye, and also from flanexti herb, likewise using the stem, steeped in warm water. Third, let him drink from cuecuechpahlli, the stem ground in our wine. Into the potion he is to drink, let there be added ingredients for a bath, from which he will emerge, having sweated out the bitter liquid of the teohamatl bark. The alder serves twice as a purging enema. First, from the juice of the root of ohuaxoco, placed in water in a tub, so that he may absorb something of it. This juice indeed expels pus from the kidneys. As a final remedy, a few doses on successive days, a preparation made from the ground herb in wine sufficient to intoxicate. As for what bocomis piu yet yields: salt, black pepper, and pepper of a pale color.

Alahuiyac tlatlonquaye

Cure for Scabies.

One who has scabies should first be washed with urine on the part of the body affected by the scabies, and then a poultice should be applied, made from the hoe-plant tlaquiim, the leaves of tlatlonquaye, the bark of the quezal elm tree, and the leaves of aquahuitl, all ground up in water.
